tagline: Interactive pattern library for boss encounter designers
aboutDescription: Why Igor Polyakov created the atlas and how its research, interactive models, translations, and open licenses are developed.
aboutIntro: Boss Fight Atlas is an interactive pattern library that helps game designers turn boss mechanics into readable, tunable, and testable systems.
aboutMotivationBody: I had been making games for only about a month. Most of my current game had already been vibe-coded and was becoming surprisingly good, but that approach stopped working when I reached the bosses. I struggled to explain what I wanted to an agent—and realized I did not yet understand what the bosses should be or what they should do.
aboutResearchBody: The catalogue starts from observed mechanics and cited sources. Categories are working navigation, not a claim that every game follows one universal taxonomy.
aboutModelsBody: Animations and the Boss Builder turn written ideas into behavior you can inspect, combine, and test.
aboutReviewBody: Eight locales share the same content contract. Automated checks protect structure; factual, design, and language accuracy still require independent human review.
aboutOpenBody: Original text and illustrations are published under CC BY 4.0, and implementation code under MIT, so the work can be studied, cited, and improved.
aboutContactBody: I am Igor Polyakov, a software engineering manager and product-minded engineer. I build systems that connect research, product decisions, and disciplined delivery.

aboutStory.atlasBody: I needed a thesaurus of familiar boss mechanics: patterns already used again and again in excellent games. I first asked a model for an illustrated list, then kept shaping it into a tool I could use without friction. The list became an atlas of {count} mechanics, although many pages are still works in progress.
aboutStory.communityBody: I wanted to share it early. The site now supports {localeCount} languages and its source is open for anyone who wants to improve the code, the design material, or a translation. I have only been making games for about a month, so please treat the material with caution: professional review is especially welcome, and feedback is useful even without a pull request.
aboutStory.prototypeTitle: From a vague request to an agent-ready brief
aboutStory.prototypeIntro: While building the atlas, I realized I wanted to throw mechanics into a basket, export a structured brief, and give it to an agent to prototype a boss. That workflow became the Boss Builder.
aboutStory.beforeText: Make a memorable gatekeeper boss with several phases. Keep it difficult but fair.
aboutStory.prototypeNote: This is an abbreviated illustration. The Builder exports versioned JSON with localized mechanic summaries, source URLs, phases, combinations, and design goals.
aboutStory.alternativesBody: Before building the atlas I looked for an existing resource. Game Mechanics and SteamMaho are broad databases covering games as a whole, while Jenova offers a dedicated AI boss-fight generator. None matched the narrow, inspectable mechanics workflow I wanted; together they also suggest that the problem is real and worth exploring.
